lessons.title: Classes and instances
lessons.tag: A fish-bread mould and fish breads
story: A class is like a mould for fish-shaped bread (bungeoppang). With just one mould you can bake as many fish breads as you like. Each fish bread that comes out is an instance (object).
The order that bakes a fish bread from the mould is new. The constructor is where you set its first shape while baking, like "fill it with red bean" or "fill it with custard".

Each fish bread keeps its own filling (instance members). But a value the whole shop has only one of, like "the number of fish breads baked today", is static (a static member). It is like everyone looking at the same single blackboard.
points: Class = the blueprint (mould), instance = the real thing made with new (it lives in heap memory)
Constructor = a special function that sets the first values when an object is made. this means "myself"
Several constructors with the same name but different parameters = overloading
static exists only once per class. Use it directly with the class name, without new (a singleton also "exists only once")
Naming rules: classes in PascalCase, fields and variables in camelCase

example.title: C# — constructor chaining and object initialisers

quiz.q: If we compare it to a fish-bread mould and fish breads, what is an "instance"?
options: The sign of the fish-bread shop
Each fish bread baked from the mould
quiz.explain: The class is the mould, and the real fish bread baked with new is the instance. Each fish bread has its own filling (field values).

quiz.q: What appears on the screen when this code runs?
quiz.explain: static Total is one blackboard everyone shares, so it goes up twice to 2. Mine belongs to each object, so b's Mine is 1.

quiz.q: What best describes the job of a constructor?
options: It cleans up when an object is deleted
It sets the first values when an object is made
quiz.explain: It is called exactly once, the moment you make an object with new, and sets up its "starting state" correctly. It is the moment you decide red bean or custard.

quiz.q: What is it called when you make several functions with the same name that differ only in the number or types of parameters?
quiz.explain: Overloading is "same name, different ingredients", like Hero() and Hero(string, int). Overriding is rewriting a parent function through inheritance, which is different.

quiz.q: Which statement about static members is wrong?
options: A new one is created every time an instance is made
You can use it directly with the class name
It stays for the whole program, so putting too much in it takes up memory
quiz.explain: Instance members are the ones created anew. static exists only once per class, so if you keep adding to a static List, memory keeps piling up (the memory-leak story from the notes!).

practice.prompt: The default constructor calls another constructor, and an object initialiser bakes one more hero. Fill in the blanks.

blanks.hint: The word that calls "another constructor of myself"
The order that bakes a fish bread from the mould

practice.explain: : this(...) means "I will leave it to my other constructor". And you need new to make a real fish bread (instance) from the mould (class).

practice.prompt: The fish-bread shop baked three. Two lines appear on the screen. What are they?
practice.hint: static is the one blackboard for the whole shop; Filling belongs to each fish bread (팥 = red bean, 슈크림 = custard)
practice.explain: Made is static, so it is a blackboard all three share. It went up three times, so 3. b's filling belongs only to b, so it is 슈크림 (custard).

lessons.title: Encapsulation (hiding information)
story: A piggy bank has only a slot for coins, and its belly is closed. That way nobody can open its belly to take money out as they like or put strange things in. This is encapsulation.
In code we hide important values with private and open only fixed slots (methods, properties) such as "put in" and "look" to the outside.

What really matters is not hiding but "keeping the rules". If someone tries to set an age of -5, the piggy bank itself must say "No!" and stop it. A promise an object always keeps like this is called an invariant.
points: private = only me, protected = me and my children, public = everyone, (C#) internal = the same project (assembly)
Getter/Setter (Java) = C# properties { get; set; }
The C# init accessor: you can set the value only when creating the object, and never change it afterwards
Check the value inside the setter to block strange values (Tell, Don't Ask: tell the object to do the work)
Hiding information means you can change the inside from an array to a hash map and the outside code stays the same (Divide and Conquer)

example.title: C# — a property that checks values

quiz.q: What is the "real" purpose of encapsulation?
options: Mechanically adding get/set to every variable
Blocking strange values so the object keeps its own rules
Putting all code into one file
quiz.explain: Leaving every get/set open is like leaving the piggy bank's belly open. The key is checking incoming values so the rules (invariants) are kept.

quiz.q: In C#, what happens on the last line of this code?
quiz.explain: init means "you can only set it while creating". If you try to change it afterwards, the compiler stops you right away.

quiz.q: Which access modifier hides something so only the same class can use it?
quiz.explain: private is "the drawer in my room". protected can be opened by children too, internal within the same project, and public by anyone.

quiz.q: When making a bank account object, which way keeps encapsulation best?
options: Leave balance public and change it freely from outside
Remove balance and calculate it every time
Keep balance private and check for negative amounts and insufficient funds inside Deposit(amount) and Withdraw(amount) methods
quiz.explain: Hide the money and open only the put-in and take-out slots (methods). Checking "no negatives" and "you cannot take out more than the balance" inside them makes the account keep its own rules.

quiz.q: Which is NOT a benefit of good encapsulation?
options: Changing the inner data structure breaks less of the outside code
The program automatically becomes twice as fast
You can block strange values in one place
It becomes easier to find where a bug came from
quiz.explain: Encapsulation makes code safe and easy to fix; it is not magic that raises speed.

practice.prompt: A property that hides the age and blocks negative values. Fill in the blanks.

blanks.hint: The access modifier that only I can open, like the drawer in my room
The name for "the newly incoming value" inside set

practice.explain: _age is hidden with private, and inside set the incoming value is called value. Because it is checked at the entrance, a strange age can never get in.

practice.prompt: Coins were put into the piggy bank. How many are inside?
practice.hint: Look carefully at the if inside Put
practice.explain: The piggy bank blocks -300 by itself (it only adds when n > 0). 500 + 100 = 600. This is the rule encapsulation protects.

lessons.title: Inheritance and overriding
story: When "A is a B" makes sense, as in "a dog is an animal", use inheritance (an is-a relationship). The child class inherits the parent's fields and methods and adds only what it needs.
If the parent made "cry" just print "...", a dog should cry "멍멍" (woof), right? A child rewriting a parent method in its own way is called overriding.

In Java every method can be rewritten (is virtual) from the start. C# is the opposite: the parent must allow it with virtual before a child can override it. Using the same name without permission becomes new (hiding), and calling it through the parent type runs the parent's version.
points: Use inheritance only when "is-a" fits. Java extends / C# : Parent
A class has only one parent (multiple inheritance is banned because of the diamond problem)
Java: virtual by default, use final to block / C#: non-virtual by default, open with virtual + override
C# new only hides the name → calling through a parent-type variable runs the parent method
Keywords that block inheritance: Java final class, C# sealed class. Calling the parent: Java super / C# base

example.title: C# — the difference between override and new

quiz.q: Which relationship fits inheritance best?
options: Cat — animal (a cat is an animal)
Student — bag (a student has a bag)
House — address (a house has an address)
quiz.explain: "A cat is an animal" makes sense, so it is is-a. "Has" is has-a, so you put it in a field instead of inheriting.

quiz.q: In C#, what does this code print? (부모 = parent, 자식 = child)
quiz.explain: virtual + override "swaps" the child method into the parent's slot. Even though the variable type is Parent, the real object is a Child, so "자식" is printed.

quiz.q: If the code above uses new instead of override (public new string Name() => "자식") and the parent's virtual is also removed, what is the result?
quiz.explain: new is "hiding" that only covers the name. Calling through a Parent-type variable runs the parent's version. If you want polymorphism, always use virtual/override!

quiz.q: Why do Java and C# allow a class to inherit from "only one parent"?
options: Because there is not enough memory
Because of the diamond problem: if two parents have methods with the same name, it is unclear which to use
quiz.explain: If mum has "cook" and dad has "cook" too, whose recipe do you follow? So a class has one parent, but it can implement several interfaces.

quiz.q: Which C# keyword stops anyone from inheriting any further?
quiz.explain: sealed means "Sealed!". In Java final class does the same. abstract is the opposite: it means you must inherit and complete it.

practice.prompt: A cat inherits from animal and swaps "cry" for 야옹 (meow). Fill in the blanks.

blanks.hint: The word the parent uses to allow "you may change this"
The one symbol that shows inheritance in C#
The word a child uses to swap in a parent method

practice.explain: In C# the parent allows it with virtual and the child swaps it in with override. Inheritance is written with a colon (:), as in class Cat : Animal. In Java it would be extends.

practice.prompt: new (hiding) and override (swapping in) are mixed. Three lines appear.
practice.hint: When the variable type is Parent, new runs the parent's and override runs the child's (멍멍 = woof)
practice.explain: p is a Parent box, so the hidden (new) Hello is the parent's "Parent". Cry is overridden, so it is the real object's (Dog) "멍멍". d is a Dog box, so "Dog".

lessons.title: Polymorphism and casting
story: The teacher says just one thing, "Everyone, make a sound!", and the dog goes woof, the cat goes meow and the duck goes quack. Each answering the same command in its own way is polymorphism.

Putting a child into a parent box (upcasting) is always safe, because a dog is always an animal. But taking a "dog" back out of an "animal" box (downcasting) is risky. There might be a cat in the box!
So before taking it out, you ask "Are you really a dog?". Java uses instanceof, and C# uses is and as. as quietly returns null if it is not, and is checks and takes it out in one go.
points: Polymorphism = the same message (method call), different behaviour for each object
Upcasting (child → parent) is always safe / downcasting (parent → child) needs a check
Java: obj instanceof Dog d / C#: obj is Dog d, obj as Dog (null if it fails)
A forced cast (Dog)obj can stop the program with an InvalidCastException if it is wrong
C# switch expression pattern matching: monster switch { Slime s => ..., Goblin g => ..., _ => ... }

example.title: C# — taking things out safely

quiz.q: What best explains "polymorphism"?
options: Calling the same method behaves differently depending on the real object
Having many variables in one class
quiz.explain: One "Make a sound!" and the dog says woof while the cat says meow. The caller is the same, but the answers differ.

quiz.q: Which of these is always safe and needs no check?
quiz.explain: A dog is always an animal, so putting it into a parent box is always safe. When taking it back out, you must check it really is that animal.

quiz.q: In C#, what is the result of this code? (비었음 = empty, 강아지 = dog)
quiz.explain: as quietly returns null instead of an error when it cannot convert. The box held text, not a dog, so it prints "비었음".

quiz.q: Which C# operator is most like Java's instanceof?
quiz.explain: Java: if (m instanceof Slime s), C#: if (m is Slime s). Both mean "Are you a slime? If so, I will call you s".

quiz.q: What is the main reason to prefer is or as over a forced cast (Dog)animal?
options: When it is wrong, the program does not stop with an exception and you can handle it safely
quiz.explain: A wrong forced cast throws an InvalidCastException. With is and as you can decide in advance "if not, do this", so they are safe.

practice.prompt: Check whether the monster in the box is a slime and take it out. Make it become null if it is not a goblin.

blanks.hint: Asks "Are you a ...?" and takes it out in one go
Quietly gives null if it cannot convert

practice.explain: is checks and takes out in one go, and as gives null instead of an error. Both are safer than a forced cast.

practice.prompt: The zoo friends were told one after another, "Make a sound!". What appears on one line?
practice.hint: The variables are all Animal, but the real objects are different (멍멍 woof, 야옹 meow, 꽥 quack)
practice.explain: It is the same a.Sound(), but each real object answers differently. That is polymorphism! 멍멍 야옹 꽥 멍멍.

lessons.title: Abstract classes and interfaces
lessons.tag: A half-finished blueprint vs a licence
story: An abstract class is a "half-finished blueprint". Every animal has a name and an age (shared fields) and breathes the same way (shared code), so those are written in advance, and only "how to cry" is left empty for the child to fill in.

An interface is a "licence". Having a "swimming licence" is a promise that you can Swim(). A duck, a person and a robot can each get a swimming licence separately. And you can hold several licences at the same time!
In short, an abstract class says "what something is (is-a)", and an interface says "what it can do (can-do)".
points: Abstract class: can have fields (state) and shared code, cannot be created directly with new, only one parent (extends)
Interface: a promise of behaviour (a contract), a class can implement several (implements / in C# separated by commas after the colon)
Interfaces have no fields (state). Java 8+ and C# 8+ allow default method implementations
C# explicit interface implementation: void IPlayer.Attack() — implement them separately when names clash
C# interface names usually start with I (IRepository, IDisposable)

example.title: C# — getting several licences

quiz.q: What is the best way to express "a duck, a person and a robot can all swim" in code?
options: Each of the three implements an ISwimmer interface
All three inherit from an abstract class called Swimmer
Merge the three into one class
quiz.explain: A duck, a person and a robot are not "the same kind (is-a)", but they share "can swim (can-do)". An interface (licence) is perfect for that.

quiz.q: Which is true about abstract classes?
options: You can create one directly with new
One class can inherit from several
It can have fields and shared code
quiz.explain: An abstract class is a half-finished blueprint, so it can hold fields like name and age and shared code in advance. But you cannot new it directly, and there is only one parent.

quiz.q: What can one class have several of at the same time?
quiz.explain: You may get many licences (interfaces), as in class Duck : Animal, ISwimmer, IFlyer. There is only one parent class!

quiz.q: When IPlayer and IMonster both have Attack(), how do you make the two Attacks separately in C#?
options: Explicit interface implementation: void IPlayer.Attack() { } / void IMonster.Attack() { }
quiz.explain: Make "attacking as a player" and "attacking as a monster" separately by putting name tags on them. When calling, choose which role you call it in, as in ((IPlayer)hc).Attack().

quiz.q: In the table from the notes, which belongs to "is-a relationship, inheriting shared code"?
quiz.explain: An abstract class gives "A is a B" and shared code through extends (inheritance), and an interface gives "the same promised ability to different classes" through implement.

practice.prompt: A duck that has both a half-finished blueprint (Animal) and a swimming licence (ISwimmer). Fill in the blanks.

blanks.hint: A "half-finished" class you cannot new directly
A method left empty without a body, saying "the child fills this in"
The name of the licence the duck got

practice.explain: Both abstract classes and abstract methods use abstract. After the single parent class, add licences (interfaces) separated by commas.

practice.prompt: Attacking as a player and attacking as a monster were made separately. Two lines appear.
practice.hint: Look in order at which role (interface) each call uses (검 = sword, 발톱 = claws)
practice.explain: First it is called in the monster role, so "발톱" (claws), then in the player role, so "검" (sword). Even with clashing names, explicit implementation makes them work separately.

lessons.title: Generics, collections and data structures
story: Generics are name tags on boxes. List<int> is "a box only for numbers", and List<string> is "a box only for text". With a name tag, the compiler catches it right away if you put in the wrong thing.

There are many kinds of boxes. A List (array) lets you take things out directly by their number tag. A Set cannot hold the same thing twice. A Map (Dictionary in C#) is a "name → item" locker, so knowing the name is enough to find it at once.

There are ways of lining up too. A Stack is a pile of plates (the last one placed comes out first, LIFO) — used for undo (Ctrl+Z). A Queue is a lunch line (first in line, first served, FIFO) — used to handle things in turn.
points: Generics = name-tag boxes whose type is decided later. C# allows List<int> (no boxing); Java needs List<Integer> (the int → Integer wrapper)
Java erases type information after compiling (Type Erasure); C# remembers it while running (Reified)
List: lookup by number O(1), inserting or deleting in the middle O(N) / LinkedList: you must walk in order to find things, but insert and delete are fast once you know the position
HashSet: no duplicates, find O(1) / Dictionary (Map): find by key O(1) — use a Dictionary when you search often
Stack (LIFO): undo, recursion / Queue (FIFO): waiting lines / Heap: taking out the largest or smallest value quickly
Big O = how much slower things get as the data grows (time and space complexity)

example.title: C# — use a Dictionary when you search often

quiz.q: Which data structure "takes out the most recent thing first", like undo (Ctrl+Z)?
quiz.explain: When you pile up plates, you take from the top (the one placed last). That is a Stack. A Queue is like a lunch line: whoever comes first goes first.

quiz.q: A game needs to find items by item name very often. What fits best?
options: Put them in a Dictionary<string, Item> with the name as the key
Put them in a List and search from start to end every time
Join them all into one string
quiz.explain: Just like the pink note in the notes! "Use a Dictionary when you search a lot, avoid loops". The name tag (key) opens the locker directly, so it is O(1).

quiz.q: How many items are in set after this code runs? (사과 = apple, 배 = pear)
quiz.explain: A Set never holds the same thing twice. "사과" stays only once, so there are 2: apple and pear.

quiz.q: Why can Java not use List<int>, so you must use List<Integer>?
options: Because Java erases generic types when compiling (Type Erasure), so it can only hold objects
quiz.explain: After compiling, Java removes the name tag and makes it "just a box of things (Object)". So an int must be wrapped in the Integer wrapper (a wrapper class). C# remembers the name tag to the end, so List<int> works.

quiz.q: What is the Big O of "taking something out directly by its number (index)" from an array (List)?
quiz.explain: An array's cells sit side by side, so "cell 5!" goes there directly. The time stays the same however much data there is, so it is O(1). But inserting in the middle means pushing everything behind it, so that is O(N).

practice.prompt: Make a locker that finds attack power directly by item name. Fill in the blanks.

blanks.hint: A "name → value" locker (Map in Java)
The method that says "give it to me if it is there, otherwise false"

practice.explain: A Dictionary finds by key directly, so O(1)! TryGetValue returns false instead of an error when the key is missing, so it is safe.

practice.prompt: 1, 2 and 3 were put in turn into a plate pile (Stack) and a lunch line (Queue), and one was taken out of each.
practice.hint: A Stack gives the last one put in; a Queue gives the first one put in
practice.explain: The Stack (LIFO) gives the top one, 3, first, and the Queue (FIFO) gives the front one, 1, first. So "3 1".

lessons.title: Object rules, record and strings
story: The grandparent of every object is Object. That is why everyone has ToString() (show as text), Equals() (compare for equality) and GetHashCode() (a locker number).

There is one rule: "If Equals says two things are equal, their locker numbers (hashCode) must be equal too." HashSet and Dictionary first find the slot by locker number and then check with Equals inside it. If the numbers differ, they search the wrong slot and cannot find it!

A string (String) cannot be changed once made (it is immutable). "Hello" + " World" does not fix the original text; it makes new text. Joining text over and over in a loop creates lots of garbage, so use StringBuilder.
points: If you override Equals, you must override GetHashCode (hashCode) along with it
C# record: automatically makes Equals, GetHashCode and ToString that treat equal values as the same (perfect for immutable data)
Comparable (IComparable): my own default order (compareTo) / Comparator (IComparer): a special sorting rule given from outside
String is immutable → use StringBuilder when joining a lot
String methods: IsEmpty · Split · ToUpper/ToLower · Length · Substring · Replace · Trim · Contains · IndexOf · EndsWith

example.title: C# — value comparison with a one-line record

quiz.q: What can happen if you override Equals but leave GetHashCode as it is?
options: Objects with the same contents cannot be found in a HashSet or Dictionary, or get added twice
quiz.explain: A HashSet first finds the slot by locker number (hashCode). If the numbers differ it searches a different slot, so even twins are reported as "not there" or added again separately.

quiz.q: In C#, what is the result of this code? (용 = dragon)
quiz.explain: A record compares by "equal values are equal". The name and power are the same, so True. If it were a plain class they would be different objects, so False.

quiz.q: Why use StringBuilder when joining text ten thousand times in a loop?
options: Because only StringBuilder can use Korean
Because a String can only hold 10 characters
Because String is immutable, so every + makes a new string and wastes a lot of memory
quiz.explain: A String is paper you cannot fix once written. Each time you add a letter you must write everything again on new paper. StringBuilder is a notebook with an eraser, so you can keep writing on.

quiz.q: You want to sort a list of students "by number by default, but by height (tallest first) just today". What do you use for "tallest first"?
options: Make a separate Comparator (IComparer) and pass it when sorting
quiz.explain: The default order you already have is Comparable, and a special rule given from outside each time is Comparator. Keep the default order and swap in only today's rule.

quiz.q: What is the value of s after this code runs?
quiz.explain: Strings are immutable, so ToUpper() only returns new text "CAT" and does not change s. To change it, store it again, as in s = s.ToUpper();.

practice.prompt: Make in one line a Point that counts equal values as the same, then make a copy with only Y changed.

blanks.hint: The word that automatically makes Equals, GetHashCode and ToString
"Copy it and change only this"

practice.explain: record automatically makes value comparison and a nice ToString. with keeps the original as it is and makes a new changed value (immutable!).

practice.prompt: Strings are immutable. Three lines appear.
practice.hint: Does ToUpper change s, or give new text?
practice.explain: ToUpper only returns the new text "HELLO", so s stays hello. ab + cd are written into the StringBuilder to make abcd, length 4.

lessons.title: Delegates, lambdas, LINQ and events
story: A delegate is "a box that holds a function". Like numbers or text, a function can be stored in a variable and sent by parcel to another function. Things you can store in a variable like this are called first-class objects.

A lambda is a short function without a name. x => x * 2 means "take x and give back twice as much". LINQ takes lambdas like these to filter a list (Where), change it (Select) and combine it into one (Aggregate).

An event is a "doorbell". The button (the sender, Emit) only goes "ding-dong!" and does not know who is listening. People who want to listen (the receivers, onEvent) register with +=, and each does their job when it rings. When done, you must unregister with -= so memory does not leak.
points: Action<T>: returns nothing / Func<T, TResult>: the last type is the return type / Predicate<T>: a check that returns bool
Lambda: (parameters) => expression. A nameless function made right on the spot
LINQ: Where (filter) · Select (change) · Any (at least one?) · Aggregate (combine into one) · ToList (run right now)
Where and Select use lazy evaluation (computed when needed); ToList and Count evaluate immediately
event: from outside only += / -= are allowed. Separating sending (Emit) and receiving (onEvent) makes changing, reusing and finding bugs easier (observer pattern, MVC)

example.title: C# — a LINQ pipeline
example.code:
var numbers = new List<int> { 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 };

var evenSquares = numbers
    .Where(n => n % 2 == 0)   // 2, 4, 6
    .Select(n => n * n)       // 4, 16, 36
    .ToList();

int sum = numbers.Aggregate(0, (acc, n) => acc + n); // 21
bool hasBig = numbers.Any(n => n > 5);               // true

quiz.q: What is the result of this LINQ?
quiz.explain: Where keeps only 3, 4 and 5, which are bigger than 2, and Select multiplies each by 10 to give 30, 40, 50. Filter → change!

quiz.q: Which C# delegate type holds "a function that takes one string, prints it and returns nothing"?
quiz.explain: Action is a function that "only does something and returns nothing". Func returns its last type, and Predicate returns true/false.

quiz.q: What is the result of this code?
quiz.explain: Aggregate rolls through them one by one and combines them. 0+1=1, 1+2=3, 3+3=6, 6+4=10. It grows like rolling a snowman.

quiz.q: Which is true about events?
options: The sender (Emit) must know every receiver and call them directly
Receivers register with +=, and must unregister with -= when done so memory does not leak
Only one listener can hear an event
From outside you can freely clear it with event = null
quiz.explain: A doorbell only has to go "ding-dong" without knowing who listens. Listeners register (+=), and if they do not unregister (-=) when moving away, they stay held and memory leaks (the yellow note in the notes!).

quiz.q: If you only write Where and Select and never call ToList(), when is it computed?
options: It is never computed and gives an error
Later, when you take the results out one by one (lazy evaluation)
quiz.explain: LINQ only writes down the "order slip", and starts cooking when you really take things out (foreach, ToList, Count). This is called lazy evaluation.

practice.prompt: A LINQ that filters only even numbers and changes them into squares. Fill in the blanks.

blanks.hint: Keep only what matches the condition (filter)
Change each one into a different shape

practice.explain: Filter with Where → change with Select → compute right now with ToList! Do not forget they start with a capital letter.

practice.prompt: Three LINQ methods were used on a list of numbers. Three lines appear.
practice.hint: The order stays the same. Any is True if there is at least one
practice.explain: Doubling 3, 8 and 6, which are bigger than 2 → 6,16,12. There is 8, which is bigger than 7, so True. Adding them all gives 3+8+1+6 = 18.

lessons.title: Exception handling and protecting memory
story: try-catch is a seat belt. If an accident (exception) happens inside try, catch takes it so the whole program does not stop. finally is the clean-up you always do, whether or not there was an accident.

Things like files and network connections must be closed after use, just like water leaks if you leave the tap running and go out. In C#, using automatically turns it off (Dispose) when the block ends.

But you must not use the seat belt instead of the steering wheel. Things that happen often, like "wrong password", should not be handled as exceptions but returned as a Result. Exceptions are only for truly unexpected accidents!
points: try: give it a go / catch: take the accident / finally: always runs / throw: report an accident on purpose
Never swallow with an empty catch; when rethrowing, use throw; not throw ex; (it keeps the record of where it happened)
using / IDisposable: automatically close resources such as files, databases and sockets
Causes of memory leaks: endlessly adding to a static List or Map, new inside loops, a singleton holding on, events never unregistered
Fixes: Remove() · Clear() · null, pair up event register/unregister, in Unity cache GetComponent once in Start (no Find every frame in Update)

example.title: C# — automatic clean-up with using

quiz.q: What does this code print?
quiz.explain: It prints A, then an accident (throw) happens, so B is skipped. catch takes it and prints C, and finally always prints D. So ACD!

quiz.q: Which is the better way to handle "the password was wrong at login"?
options: Throw an exception with throw and take it with catch
Return it as a result, like Result.failure(WRONG_CREDENTIALS)
quiz.explain: A wrong password is an "expected failure" that happens every day. Exceptions are slow and hide the flow. Returning a Result means the receiver handles it without missing it. c-master does it this way too!

quiz.q: What does C#'s using (IDisposable) do?
options: When the block ends, it automatically closes resources such as files and connections
quiz.explain: It is an automatic tap shut-off. Whether it ends normally or with an accident, Dispose() is called, so resources do not leak.

quiz.q: Which is NOT a case that easily causes memory leaks?
options: Only ever adding to a static List and never removing
Only doing += on an event and never -=
Calling Clear() on a list you are done with
Repeatedly doing new for big objects inside a loop
quiz.explain: Clear() and Remove() are actually the fix. The other three are the typical leak causes in the yellow note of the notes.

quiz.q: Where is it best to call GameObject.Find in Unity?
options: Update() — find it again every frame
Awake() or Start() — find it once and store it in a variable (caching)
quiz.explain: Update is called dozens of times a second. Calling Find there every time hurts performance. It is better to find it once at the start and keep using it (the first page of the notes!).

practice.prompt: An accident happens when a score is put into a cell that does not exist. Fill in the blanks to take the accident and always clean up.

blanks.hint: The net that catches a falling accident
The clean-up you always do, accident or not

practice.explain: The array only has cells 0–2, so putting something in cell 5 is an accident! catch takes it and prints "칸이 없어요" (no such cell), and finally always prints "정리 끝" (clean-up done).

practice.prompt: 6 was divided by 0. Four lines appear. Think carefully about the order of finally and return.
practice.hint: Even when return is reached, finally runs first before leaving the function
practice.explain: "시작" (start) → an accident while dividing by 0 → catch prints "0으로 못 나눠요" (cannot divide by 0) and tries to return -1 → just before leaving, finally prints "정리" (clean-up) → outside, -1 is printed.

lessons.title: Serialisation, HTTP and asynchronous code
lessons.tag: Packing parcels and not waiting around
story: To send an object inside a program to another computer, you must pack it into a box. Packing object → text (JSON) is serialisation (Serialize), and unpacking it back into an object after receiving is deserialisation (Deserialize).

To talk to a server we use HTTP. GET means "show me", POST "make a new one", PUT "replace it all", PATCH "change part of it" and DELETE "remove it". The reply number 200 is success, 404 is not found and 500 is a broken server.

If you stand staring at the pot until the ramen water boils (synchronous), you cannot do anything else. Putting the water on and taking out the kimchi meanwhile (asynchronous) is smart. That is exactly async/await. The screen (main thread) does not freeze.
points: Data formats: CSV (tables) → XML (tags) → JSON (key-value, today's standard)
GET read · POST create (login, order) · PUT replace all · PATCH change part · DELETE remove / 200 · 404 · 500
TCP: connects and delivers reliably (email, files, slow) / UDP: fast without connecting (real-time games, video)
async/await: do other work while waiting. Wait for several at once with Task.WhenAll
No async void (only for event handlers), no blocking waits with .Result or .Wait() (deadlock), reuse HttpClient instead of new every time
In Unity, write asynchronous code with UniTask rather than coroutines

example.title: C# — waiting for two at once

quiz.q: What turns an object into JSON text so it can be sent over the network?
quiz.explain: Packing before sending is serialisation, and unpacking after receiving is deserialisation. It is like wrapping and opening a parcel.

quiz.q: Which HTTP method is mainly used to "send data to the server with a new request", as in login or ordering?
quiz.explain: POST is a request that sends data in an envelope. The notes even say "Post — request with Data — login, order"!

quiz.q: Which number does the server reply with when it says "there is no such address"?
quiz.explain: 200 is success, 404 is Not Found, and 500 is when the inside of the server is broken.

quiz.q: For something like a real-time battle game that "may lose a little but must be fast", what fits?
quiz.explain: UDP throws data quickly without checking, so it is fast. Things that must not lose a single piece, like email and files, use TCP.

quiz.q: What must you NOT do in asynchronous code?
options: Block and wait with .Result in screen code
Wait for several tasks together with Task.WhenAll
quiz.explain: .Result and .Wait() are "standing frozen in front of the ramen". The screen freezes, and a deadlock can happen where things wait for each other forever.

practice.prompt: Fetch the hero and the items at the same time and unpack the received JSON into an object. Fill in the blanks.

blanks.hint: The mark saying "I will wait inside this function"
Waiting without freezing the screen
Unpacking text (JSON) → an object

practice.explain: Wait with await inside an async function. Task.WhenAll waits for both at once! Unpacking received text into an object is deserialisation (Deserialize).

practice.prompt: Put the ramen water on and take out the kimchi while waiting. In what order do the four lines appear?
answers:
물 올림
김치 꺼냄
라면 완성
먹자!
practice.hint: An async function runs right away until its first await, and lets go there for a moment
practice.explain: It does "물 올림" (water on) right away, and while waiting its hands are free, so "김치 꺼냄" (kimchi out). When the water boils, "라면 완성" (ramen ready), and after all the waiting, "먹자!" (let's eat!). That is asynchronous code.

lessons.title: Splitting the data layers
lessons.tag: DataSource → DTO → Mapper → Model → Repository → Service
story: Think of a restaurant. The DataSource is the person who buys ingredients at the market exactly as they are. They even bring carrots with soil still on them (DTO).

The Mapper is in charge of preparing. It shakes off the soil, throws away bad pieces and fills in default ingredients when something is missing, making clean ingredients (Model). The Repository is the storekeeper. When you say "carrots, please", it checks the fridge (cache), fetches from the market if there are none, and hands out only prepared ingredients.

The Service is the chef. It judges rules such as "are there enough ingredients?" and "can this customer order?". In StarCraft terms, the SCV carrying minerals is the Repository, the brain that decides "you need 50 minerals to make a marine!" is the Service, and the marine button is the View.
points: View (screen) → Service (judges rules) → Repository (picks out data) → DataSource (talks to storage)
DTO = a shell shaped exactly like the server JSON (nullable, may have ?)
Model = clean data the app trusts and uses (non-nullable, record recommended)
Mapper = converts DTO → Model. null becomes a default value (dto.Name ?? "No name")
Make the Repository an interface → easy to swap in a fake (Mock) DataSource for tests (if storage moves between local and server, only the DataSource changes)
Split Services by domain, not by screen (ProgressService O, HomeScreenService X)

example.title: C# — preparing data with a Mapper

quiz.q: Which layer judges the rule "you can make a marine only when you have at least 50 minerals"?
quiz.explain: The SCV (Repository) only carries minerals; the brain, the Service, does the judging. That way the same rule applies whichever screen you press it on.

quiz.q: The name field in the server JSON came back empty (null). Where is it filled with a default name to make a clean Model?
quiz.explain: The Mapper is in charge of preparing! Like dto.RawName ?? "Unknown", it turns null into a default value so the Model can always be trusted.

quiz.q: What is the main reason to keep DTOs and Models separate?
options: So that when the server JSON shape changes, less of the app's inner code (rules, screens) breaks
quiz.explain: Even if the server renames user_name to nickname, you only need to fix the DTO and the Mapper. The dozens of places that use the Model stay as they are. It works like a firewall.

quiz.q: Which describes what the Repository below does?
options: It draws a Pokémon on the screen
It checks the cache first, and if missing, fetches from the DataSource, converts to a Model and returns it
quiz.explain: The storekeeper opens the fridge (cache) first, and if it is not there, goes to the market (DataSource) and hands out prepared ingredients (Model). The Service does not need to know where the data came from.

quiz.q: What is a good way to split Services?
options: One per domain (the job it does) (ProgressService, WalletService)
quiz.explain: Splitting by screen makes rule code shake whenever a screen changes, and the same rule gets copied to many screens. Split by job, like "wallet rules" and "progress rules".

practice.prompt: A Mapper (extension method) that prepares a DTO into a clean Model. Fill in the blanks.

blanks.hint: The extension-method mark that lets you call it like dto.ToModel()
The two-symbol operator meaning "if the left is null, use the right"

practice.explain: this before the first parameter marks an extension method, so you call it as dto.ToModel(). ?? is a preparing tool that turns null into a default value.

practice.prompt: Two Pokémon came from the server, but one was empty. After the Mapper, two lines appear.
practice.hint: What does the Mapper in the fill-in-the-blank problem above turn null into?
practice.explain: Pikachu stays as it is, and the Mapper fills the empty data with the name "Unknown" and experience 0. So the Model can always be trusted.

lessons.title: The Result pattern and unit tests
lessons.tag: Success boxes, failure boxes and small tests
story: Result is like having two kinds of gift box. The Success box holds the result (Data), and the Failure box holds a note saying "why it did not work" (Error). The receiver checks which box it is before opening it, so a failure is never missed by accident.
In C# we make only two types under abstract record Result: sealed record Success and sealed record Failure. Because they are sealed, no other kind of box can sneak in.

A unit test is a small quiz for each function. Write it in the order Given (in this situation) - When (if we do this) - Then (this should happen). Plugging in a fake (Mock) instead of the real server makes it fast and always gives the same result.
points: Result = Success(Data) or Failure(Error). Return expected failures as values instead of exceptions
record: value comparison, immutable / sealed: no more inheritance → only success and failure
Given - When - Then (= Arrange - Act - Assert), check the result with assert
F.I.R.S.T: fast · independent of each other · always the same result · decides pass/fail by itself · written on time
A good test = equivalence partitioning + boundary values (0, exactly the limit, limit + 1) + failure cases (null, empty values)
White box (checks the logic inside the code) / black box (checks only input → output). Mock (checks calls) · Stub (fixed values) · Fake (a simple imitation of the real thing)

example.title: C# — Result and pattern matching

quiz.q: What is the best thing about the Result pattern?
options: You end up using null a lot
It shows in the return type that it can fail, so the receiver does not forget to handle failure
quiz.explain: The box says "success or failure" on the outside, so whoever opens it must think about both cases. It is much safer than hiding failure with null.

quiz.q: Why put sealed on Result's Success and Failure?
options: So nobody can secretly make a third kind of result — it stays fixed at exactly two
quiz.explain: sealed means "sealed". A result is either success or failure, exactly two kinds, so a switch can handle every case.

quiz.q: What is the right order for writing a test?
quiz.explain: Given (in this situation) → When (if we do this) → Then (this should happen). It reads like a story, so you can tell at once what is being tested.

quiz.q: When testing "you get all the experience if you solve it within the 600-second limit", which boundary values must you include?
quiz.explain: Bugs hide at boundaries. Mixing up "at most" and "less than" makes it wrong at 600 seconds. Always test exactly-at and one-over.

quiz.q: Which is NOT a reason to plug in a fake (Mock) DataSource instead of the real server in tests?
options: You can test without the internet
It gives the same result whenever you run it
To delete the real server data
quiz.explain: With a fake, tests are fast (Fast), independent (Independent) and always give the same result (Repeatable). Not touching real data is actually the point!

practice.prompt: Add comments that split a unit test in story order. Fill in three English words.

blanks.hint: Prepare (Arrange)
Run (Act)
Check (Assert)

practice.explain: Given (situation) → When (run) → Then (check). Splitting it like this makes the test read like a story, so you see at a glance what is being tested.

practice.prompt: We tried to make marines with 80 and 30 minerals. Opening the Result boxes shows two lines.
answers:
마린 생산! 남은 미네랄 30
실패: 미네랄 부족
practice.hint: 80 is at least 50, and 30 is less than 50
practice.explain: For 80 the success box holds 80-50=30, and for 30 the failure box holds the note "미네랄 부족" (not enough minerals). The switch checks the box kind and opens it.

lessons.title: SOLID and design principles
story: Good code is like a tidy room. Each drawer holds only one kind of thing (SRP), and when something new comes along you add another drawer instead of breaking the old ones (OCP).

It would be a problem if a "toy duck" took the place of a "duck" and did not float, right? A child must keep the same promises when put in the parent's place (LSP). Do not put 100 unused buttons on a remote control, only the ones you need (ISP), and do not glue the TV to the wall but plug it into a socket (an interface) (DIP). Then you can change the TV without breaking the wall.

Add DRY (no repeating the same code), good names, high cohesion (one class focuses on one thing) and low coupling (less tangled together), and you get code that is easy to fix and reuse. MVC is the same idea. Model, View and Controller each do only their own job, so they can be attached to a different UI as they are.
points: S Single responsibility: a class has one reason to change
O Open-closed: open for extension, closed for modification
L Liskov substitution: a child keeps the promises when put in the parent's place (is-a)
I Interface segregation: split into small pieces so nobody depends on methods they do not use
D Dependency inversion: depend on interfaces, not concrete classes (inject through the constructor)
DRY · clear names · high cohesion · low coupling / design patterns: strategy · observer · facade · factory

example.title: C# — dependency inversion (DIP) and constructor injection

quiz.q: If one class draws the screen, saves files and calculates scores, which principle does it break?
quiz.explain: It is like putting socks, spoons and pencils all in one drawer. Fixing one thing easily breaks another. Split classes so each does one job.

quiz.q: Which principle makes it possible to add a new payment method (KakaoPay) by only adding a new class, without touching existing code?
quiz.explain: It is adding another drawer without breaking the chest of drawers. With an IPayment interface, you only need to make a new KakaoPay class.

quiz.q: PokemonService does not make new PokemonRepositoryImpl() itself but receives an IPokemonRepository through its constructor. Which principle is this?
quiz.explain: It plugs the TV into a socket (interface) instead of gluing it to the wall. Thanks to that, a fake Repository can be plugged in for tests.

quiz.q: What is good design regarding "cohesion and coupling"?
quiz.explain: One class sticks tightly to one thing (high cohesion) and connects loosely to other classes (low coupling). Then changing one shakes the others less.

quiz.q: In the MVC picture from the notes, what does the View do?
options: It stores data and calculates rules
It changes the server database directly
It shows the screen and sends a signal when user input comes (Emit)
quiz.explain: The View shows things and only sends the signal "the button was pressed!" (Emit). The Controller receives it (onEvent) and changes the Model, and when the Model changes it tells the View with an event. Splitting it this way makes changing, reusing and finding bugs easy.

practice.prompt: Make the service depend on a "socket" (interface) instead of a concrete class. Fill in the blanks.

blanks.hint: The word that defines a promise of behaviour (a contract)
What the constructor receives is not a concrete class but…

practice.explain: Dependency inversion (DIP)! The service only knows the socket called IPokemonRepository. Whether it is the real storage or a test fake, you just plug it in.

practice.prompt: The shop code stayed the same and only the payment method was swapped (open-closed). Two lines appear.
practice.hint: The shop just follows whichever payment is plugged in (카드 = card, 카카오 = Kakao)
practice.explain: It is the same Shop code, but depending on the plugged-in payment method it prints "카드 1000" and "카카오 500". Even when a new payment comes along, Shop is not changed; you just add a class (OCP + DIP).
